claim: Odors are intimately tied to the taste system to aid food selection and determine the sensory experience of food.
source: Odors are intimately tied to the taste system to aid food selection and determine the sensory experience of food.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about chemosensory systems.

claim: Odors alone activate gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) in Drosophila.
source: We show in Drosophila that odors alone activate gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs), trigger proboscis extension reflex (PER), a canonical taste-evoked feeding behavior, and enhance food intake.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging and electrophysiological data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Odors trigger proboscis extension reflex (PER), a canonical taste-evoked feeding behavior.
source: We show in Drosophila that odors alone activate gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs), trigger proboscis extension reflex (PER), a canonical taste-evoked feeding behavior, and enhance food intake.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing odor-evoked PER in Figure 1.

claim: Odors enhance food intake in Drosophila.
source: We show in Drosophila that odors alone activate gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs), trigger proboscis extension reflex (PER), a canonical taste-evoked feeding behavior, and enhance food intake.
evidence: This claim is supported by food consumption assay data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Odor-evoked PER requires the function of sugar-sensing GRNs.
source: Odor-evoked PER requires the function of sugar-sensing GRNs but not olfactory organs.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic silencing experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Odor-evoked PER does not require olfactory organs.
source: Odor-evoked PER requires the function of sugar-sensing GRNs but not olfactory organs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments where olfactory organs were removed, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GRNs directly respond to odors as shown by calcium imaging.
source: Calcium imaging and electrophysiological recording show that GRNs directly respond to odors.
evidence: This claim is supported by two-photon calcium imaging data in Figure 3.

claim: GRNs directly respond to odors as shown by electrophysiological recording.
source: Calcium imaging and electrophysiological recording show that GRNs directly respond to odors.
evidence: This claim is supported by tip recording data in Figure 4.

claim: Odor-evoked PER is mediated by the Gr5a receptor.
source: Odor-evoked PER is mediated by the Gr5a receptor, and is bidirectionally modulated by olfactory binding proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using Gr5a mutants shown in Figures 2H and 3H.

claim: Odor-evoked PER is bidirectionally modulated by olfactory binding proteins.
source: Odor-evoked PER is mediated by the Gr5a receptor, and is bidirectionally modulated by olfactory binding proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments of various OBPs shown in Figure 2I-K and supplementary figures.

claim: Odors and sucrose co-applied to GRNs synergistically enhance PER.
source: Finally, odors and sucrose co-applied to GRNs synergistically enhance PER and food consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by multisensory stimulation experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Odors and sucrose co-applied to GRNs synergistically enhance food consumption.
source: Finally, odors and sucrose co-applied to GRNs synergistically enhance PER and food consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by food consumption assay data in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Unified chemosensory experience is a product of layered integration in peripheral neurons and in the brain.
source: These results reveal a cell-intrinsic mechanism for odor-taste multimodal integration that takes place as early as in GRNs, indicating that unified chemosensory experience is a product of layered integration in peripheral neurons and in the brain.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings showing both peripheral and central contributions to odor-evoked PER.

claim: Olfactory and gustatory systems prime feeding by signaling food presence.
source: Olfactory and gustatory systems prime feeding by signaling food presence, guiding food choice, and inducing anticipatory responses in digestive organs (Boesveldt and de Graaf, 2017; McCrickerd and Forde, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Olfactory and gustatory systems guide food choice.
source: Olfactory and gustatory systems prime feeding by signaling food presence, guiding food choice, and inducing anticipatory responses in digestive organs (Boesveldt and de Graaf, 2017; McCrickerd and Forde, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Olfactory and gustatory systems induce anticipatory responses in digestive organs.
source: Olfactory and gustatory systems prime feeding by signaling food presence, guiding food choice, and inducing anticipatory responses in digestive organs (Boesveldt and de Graaf, 2017; McCrickerd and Forde, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Olfactory and gustatory systems synergistically define the sensory experience of food during consumption.
source: During consumption, they synergistically define the sensory experience of food together with other cues (Spence, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Imaging studies have identified neural correlates of odor-taste interaction in the brain.
source: Although imaging studies have identified neural correlates of odor-taste interaction in the brain (Small, 2012), a mechanistic understanding of chemosensory integration is still lacking.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A mechanistic understanding of chemosensory integration is still lacking.
source: Although imaging studies have identified neural correlates of odor-taste interaction in the brain (Small, 2012), a mechanistic understanding of chemosensory integration is still lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the cited literature.

claim: Peripheral chemosensory systems in Drosophila are well-characterized.
source: Drosophila offers an attractive model to address this issue, where peripheral chemosensory systems are well-characterized (Scott, 2018; Wilson, 2013), and feeding behavior can be quantified by measuring the strength of PER (Dethier, 1976) and the amount of subsequent food consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Feeding behavior in Drosophila can be quantified by measuring the strength of PER.
source: Drosophila offers an attractive model to address this issue, where peripheral chemosensory systems are well-characterized (Scott, 2018; Wilson, 2013), and feeding behavior can be quantified by measuring the strength of PER (Dethier, 1976) and the amount of subsequent food consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Feeding behavior in Drosophila can be quantified by measuring the amount of food consumption.
source: Drosophila offers an attractive model to address this issue, where peripheral chemosensory systems are well-characterized (Scott, 2018; Wilson, 2013), and feeding behavior can be quantified by measuring the strength of PER (Dethier, 1976) and the amount of subsequent food consumption.
evidence: This is a statement about established methods in the field.

claim: PER is an initial step of feeding evoked by the presentation of sugar to the proboscis or legs housing GRNs.
source: PER is an initial step of feeding evoked by the presentation of sugar to the proboscis or legs housing GRNs.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in Drosophila feeding behavior.

claim: Previous studies reported that odors increase the rate of PER.
source: Previous studies reported that odors increase the rate of PER (Oh et al., 2021; Reisenman and Scott, 2019; Shiraiwa, 2008) as well as food intake (Reisenman and Scott, 2019), exemplifying olfactory enhancement of feeding in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies reported that odors increase food intake.
source: Previous studies reported that odors increase the rate of PER (Oh et al., 2021; Reisenman and Scott, 2019; Shiraiwa, 2008) as well as food intake (Reisenman and Scott, 2019), exemplifying olfactory enhancement of feeding in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Olfactory receptor neurons are involved in odor-evoked PER.
source: However, aside from the involvement of olfactory receptor neurons (Oh et al., 2021; Shiraiwa, 2008), biological mechanisms underlying this multisensory enhancement remain elusive.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Biological mechanisms underlying multisensory enhancement of feeding remain elusive.
source: However, aside from the involvement of olfactory receptor neurons (Oh et al., 2021; Shiraiwa, 2008), biological mechanisms underlying this multisensory enhancement remain elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field based on cited literature.

claim: Multisensory integration commences at the very periphery in Drosophila.
source: Here, we investigated the impact of odors on feeding behavior and found direct contribution of GRNs to odor-evoked PER, odor-taste integration, and odor-driven enhancement of food consumption, indicating that multisensory integration commences at the very periphery.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings showing GRN responses to odors.

claim: Different odors evoked PER with different probability.
source: Different odors evoked PER with different probability (Figure 1E), latency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and duration (Figure 1F and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Different odors evoked PER with different latency.
source: Different odors evoked PER with different probability (Figure 1E), latency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and duration (Figure 1F and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Different odors evoked PER with different duration.
source: Different odors evoked PER with different probability (Figure 1E), latency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and duration (Figure 1F and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1F, 1G, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Stimulus-triggered PER was not observed in response to solvents or air.
source: Stimulus-triggered PER was not observed in response to solvents or air (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1D-G.

claim: Odors evoked PER even at the concentration of 10–2.
source: Odors evoked PER even at the concentration of 10–2, which induces stimulus-specific activity in the olfactory pathway (Badel et al., 2016; Endo et al., 2020; Kato et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in the manuscript and citations to previous literature about olfactory pathway activity.

claim: The level of PER did not correlate with the innate value of odors.
source: The level of PER did not correlate with the innate value of odors, previously determined by quantifying the odor preference of flies in a behavioral arena (Badel et al., 2016; Pearson's R=0.33, p=0.52).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data and comparison with previously published odor preference data.

claim: Odor-evoked PER was observed in other genetic backgrounds.
source: Odor-evoked PER was observed in other genetic backgrounds and another Drosophila species as well, albeit at a lower level with different tuning (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Odor-evoked PER was observed in another Drosophila species.
source: Odor-evoked PER was observed in other genetic backgrounds and another Drosophila species as well, albeit at a lower level with different tuning (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Odor-evoked PER resembled taste-evoked PER in trajectory.
source: Odor-evoked PER resembled taste-evoked PER in multiple aspects. First, its trajectory was similar to that of taste-evoked PER (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1—video 1) and was consistent with the reported movement of proboscis during sucrose-evoked PER (Schwarz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and comparison with published literature.

claim: The trajectories of odor-evoked PER were indistinguishable between the tested odors.
source: The trajectories were indistinguishable between the tested odors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Odor-evoked PER showed concentration dependency.
source: Second, it showed concentration dependency (Dethier, 1976; Wang et al., 2004). The probability and duration of PER increased as a function of stimulus concentration (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1E and 1G, and citations to previous literature.

claim: The probability of PER increased as a function of stimulus concentration.
source: The probability and duration of PER increased as a function of stimulus concentration (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The duration of PER increased as a function of stimulus concentration.
source: The probability and duration of PER increased as a function of stimulus concentration (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Odor-evoked PER depended on the metabolic state.
source: Third, it depended on the metabolic state just as taste-evoked PER (Inagaki et al., 2014). The duration of PER was higher in starved as compared to fed flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous literature.

claim: The duration of PER was higher in starved as compared to fed flies.
source: The duration of PER was higher in starved as compared to fed flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Removal of olfactory organs attenuated but did not eliminate odor-evoked PER.
source: To confirm that this behavior is mediated by the olfactory system, we repeated the experiment after removing the sensory organs housing the olfactory receptor neurons, namely the antennae and the maxillary palps. However, this manipulation only attenuated and did not eliminate odor-evoked PER (Figure 2A), suggesting that the olfactory system modulates but is not required for odor-evoked PER.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The olfactory system modulates but is not required for odor-evoked PER.
source: However, this manipulation only attenuated and did not eliminate odor-evoked PER (Figure 2A), suggesting that the olfactory system modulates but is not required for odor-evoked PER.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Suppression of Gr5a GRNs significantly reduced odor-evoked PER.
source: Suppression of Gr5a GRNs significantly reduced odor-evoked PER, indicating that sweet-sensing neurons detect odors and drive PER (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic silencing experiments shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Sweet-sensing neurons detect odors and drive PER.
source: Suppression of Gr5a GRNs significantly reduced odor-evoked PER, indicating that sweet-sensing neurons detect odors and drive PER (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the genetic silencing experiments shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Gr5a GRNs detect sugar and mediate food acceptance behaviors, including PER.
source: Gr5a GRNs detect sugar and mediate food acceptance behaviors, including PER (Dahanukar et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bitter-sensing Gr66a GRNs inhibit sweet-evoked PER.
source: Bitter-sensing Gr66a GRNs, on the other hand, have been shown to inhibit sweet-evoked PER (Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Expression of Kir2.1 in Gr66a neurons had little effect on odor-evoked PER in starved flies.
source: However, expression of Kir2.1 in these neurons had little effect (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2B and 2D.

claim: Gr66a pathway is downregulated in a starved condition.
source: We hypothesized that this is due to our use of starved flies because Gr66a pathway is reported to be downregulated in a starved condition (Devineni et al., 2019; Inagaki et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Flies with Gr66a GRNs silenced showed increased PER to odors in a fed state.
source: Indeed, flies of the same genotype showed increased PER to odors in a fed state (Figure 2G), indicating that Gr66a GRNs counteract PER.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Gr66a GRNs counteract PER.
source: Indeed, flies of the same genotype showed increased PER to odors in a fed state (Figure 2G), indicating that Gr66a GRNs counteract PER.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental results shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Water and low salt can induce PER.
source: Two other tastes, water and low salt can also induce PER (Cameron et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2004), which are detected by Ppk28 and Ir94e GRNs, respectively (Cameron et al., 2010; Jaeger et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Water is detected by Ppk28 GRNs.
source: Two other tastes, water and low salt can also induce PER (Cameron et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2004), which are detected by Ppk28 and Ir94e GRNs, respectively (Cameron et al., 2010; Jaeger et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Low salt is detected by Ir94e GRNs.
source: Two other tastes, water and low salt can also induce PER (Cameron et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2004), which are detected by Ppk28 and Ir94e GRNs, respectively (Cameron et al., 2010; Jaeger et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Suppression of Ppk28 GRNs did not affect odor-evoked PER.
source: However, suppression of these cell types did not affect odor-evoked PER (Figure 2B, E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2B and 2E.

claim: Suppression of Ir94e GRNs did not affect odor-evoked PER.
source: However, suppression of these cell types did not affect odor-evoked PER (Figure 2B, E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2B and 2F.

claim: Gr5a GRNs enhance odor-evoked PER.
source: Together, Gr5a GRNs enhance, whereas Gr66a GRNs inhibit odor-evoked PER.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Gr66a GRNs inhibit odor-evoked PER.
source: Together, Gr5a GRNs enhance, whereas Gr66a GRNs inhibit odor-evoked PER.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental results shown in Figure 2.

claim: GRNs are housed in multiple external organs, including the labella at the tip of proboscis, the legs, the wing margins, and the ovipositor.
source: As GRNs are housed in multiple external organs, including the labella at the tip of proboscis, the legs, the wing margins, and the ovipositor (Scott, 2018), we next sought to narrow down the GRNs responsible for odor-evoked PER.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Removal of the legs and wings did not abolish odor-evoked PER.
source: We found that removal of the legs and wings did not abolish the behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activation of the ovipositor induces egg laying rather than PER.
source: Moreover, activation of the ovipositor induces egg laying rather than PER (Dethier, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: GRNs act predominantly in the labella to induce odor-evoked PER.
source: These results suggest that GRNs act predominantly in the labella to induce odor-evoked PER.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental results showing that removal of legs and wings did not abolish the behavior.

claim: GRNs do not express olfactory receptors.
source: Because GRNs do not express olfactory receptors (Davie et al., 2018; Li et al., 2021; Scott et al., 2001), either gustatory receptors or some other molecules are likely to interact with odorants (Jones et al., 2007; Kwon et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Gustatory receptors or some other molecules are likely to interact with odorants in GRNs.
source: Because GRNs do not express olfactory receptors (Davie et al., 2018; Li et al., 2021; Scott et al., 2001), either gustatory receptors or some other molecules are likely to interact with odorants (Jones et al., 2007; Kwon et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the fact that GRNs do not express olfactory receptors but respond to odors, supported by citations.

claim: Odor-evoked PER was nearly undetectable in the Gr5a mutant.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, odor-evoked PER was nearly undetectable in the Gr5a mutant but spared in the control (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Gr5a receptor is necessary for odor-evoked PER.
source: This demonstrates that Gr5a receptor is necessary for odor-evoked PER.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Odorant binding proteins (OBPs) are thought to bind and help transport hydrophobic odorants to chemosensory receptors through aqueous lymph.
source: Odorant binding proteins (OBPs) are another set of molecules that could mediate odor detection by GRNs. They are thought to bind and help transport hydrophobic odorants to chemosensory receptors through aqueous lymph (Larter et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: OBPs are expressed in taste as well as olfactory sensilla.
source: OBPs are expressed in taste as well as olfactory sensilla (Galindo and Smith, 2001) and modulate sugar-evoked PER (Swarup et al., 2014), raising the possibility that those in the taste sensilla also mediate odorant detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: OBPs modulate sugar-evoked PER.
source: OBPs are expressed in taste as well as olfactory sensilla (Galindo and Smith, 2001) and modulate sugar-evoked PER (Swarup et al., 2014), raising the possibility that those in the taste sensilla also mediate odorant detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Knockdown of Obp18a decreased odor-evoked PER.
source: Knockdown of Obp18a, Obp57d/e, and Obp57e genes decreased, whereas that of Obp49a gene increased odor-evoked PER (Figure 2I﻿﻿ and J, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Knockdown of Obp57d/e decreased odor-evoked PER.
source: Knockdown of Obp18a, Obp57d/e, and Obp57e genes decreased, whereas that of Obp49a gene increased odor-evoked PER (Figure 2I﻿﻿ and J, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Knockdown of Obp57e decreased odor-evoked PER.
source: Knockdown of Obp18a, Obp57d/e, and Obp57e genes decreased, whereas that of Obp49a gene increased odor-evoked PER (Figure 2I﻿﻿ and J, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Knockdown of Obp49a increased odor-evoked PER.
source: Knockdown of Obp18a, Obp57d/e, and Obp57e genes decreased, whereas that of Obp49a gene increased odor-evoked PER (Figure 2I﻿﻿ and J, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Knockdown of Obp19b, Obp56g, Obp56h, Obp57a/c, and Obp83c genes did not have a significant effect on odor-evoked PER.
source: Knockdown of Obp19b, Obp56g, Obp56h, Obp57a/c, and Obp83c genes did not have a significant effect on odor-evoked PER (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The increased PER following Obp49a knockdown likely reflects disinhibition of sweet-sensing GRNs.
source: The increased PER following Obp49a knockdown likely reflects disinhibition of sweet-sensing GRNs as Obp49a mediates the inhibitory impact of bitter chemicals on the activity of sweet-sensing GRNs (Jeong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental results and citation to previous literature.

claim: Obp49a mediates the inhibitory impact of bitter chemicals on the activity of sweet-sensing GRNs.
source: The increased PER following Obp49a knockdown likely reflects disinhibition of sweet-sensing GRNs as Obp49a mediates the inhibitory impact of bitter chemicals on the activity of sweet-sensing GRNs (Jeong et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: OBPs modulate odor detection by GRNs.
source: These results suggest that OBPs modulate odor detection by GRNs.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Robust odor responses were observed in Gr5a and Gr66a GRNs.
source: Consistent with the contribution of Gr5a and Gr66a GRNs to odor-evoked PER, robust odor responses were observed in these neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Gr5a and Gr66a GRNs responded to all the tested odors but not to control stimuli.
source: They responded to all the tested odors but not to control stimuli, with distinct tuning (Figure 3B–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3B-F and supplementary figures.

claim: Gr5a and Gr66a GRNs responded to odors with distinct tuning.
source: They responded to all the tested odors but not to control stimuli, with distinct tuning (Figure 3B–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3B-F and supplementary figures.

claim: Gr5a and Gr66a GRNs responded to odors in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: They responded to all the tested odors but not to control stimuli, with distinct tuning (Figure 3B–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: A linear combination of Gr5a and Gr66a GRN responses well predicted the magnitude of odor-evoked PER.
source: A linear combination of Gr5a and Gr66a GRN responses well predicted the magnitude of odor-evoked PER with the former and the latter contributing to enhancement and suppression of PER, respectively (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Gr5a GRN responses contribute to enhancement of PER.
source: A linear combination of Gr5a and Gr66a GRN responses well predicted the magnitude of odor-evoked PER with the former and the latter contributing to enhancement and suppression of PER, respectively (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Gr66a GRN responses contribute to suppression of PER.
source: A linear combination of Gr5a and Gr66a GRN responses well predicted the magnitude of odor-evoked PER with the former and the latter contributing to enhancement and suppression of PER, respectively (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Odor and sucrose responses were positively correlated in Gr5a GRNs.
source: Odor and sucrose responses were positively correlated in Gr5a GRNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Ppk28 and Ir94e GRNs did not respond to any odors.
source: By contrast, Ppk28 and Ir94e GRNs did not respond to any odors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J and K), matching their little contribution to odor-evoked PER (Figure 2B, F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J and K.

claim: Covering the maxillary palps had little effect on odor responses of GRNs.
source: This manipulation had little effect on the odor responses (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3D and 3F.

claim: Covering the labella eliminated odor responses of GRNs.
source: On the other hand, the responses were eliminated after covering the labella (Figure 3D and F), demonstrating that GRNs themselves sense odors.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 3D and 3F.

claim: GRNs themselves sense odors.
source: On the other hand, the responses were eliminated after covering the labella (Figure 3D and F), demonstrating that GRNs themselves sense odors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing that covering the labella eliminated odor responses.

claim: Odor responses were absent in the Gr5a mutant.
source: We found that odor responses were absent in the Gr5a mutant but spared in control flies (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Odor responses in Gr5a GRNs depend on Gr5a receptor.
source: This confirms that odor responses in Gr5a GRNs depend on Gr5a receptor.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results shown in Figure 3H.

claim: L-type sensilla housing a sweet-sensing GRN robustly responded to sucrose and two tested odors.
source: L-type sensilla housing a sweet-sensing GRN robustly responded to sucrose, but also to two tested odors, 4-methylcyclohexanol and banana odor, at a rate higher than the solvent (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by tip recording data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: I-type sensilla housing sweet- and bitter-sensing GRNs responded to odors.
source: I-type sensilla housing sweet- and bitter-sensing GRNs also responded to odors (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by tip recording data shown in Figures 4A and 4C.

claim: Recording from specific types of GRNs using calcium imaging and specific types of taste sensilla using tip recording together demonstrates that GRNs in the labella sense odors.
source: In sum, recording from specific types of GRNs using calcium imaging and specific types of taste sensilla using tip recording together demonstrates that GRNs in the labella sense odors in line with a recent study using a different electrophysiological technique (Dweck and Carlson, 2023).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental results shown in Figures 3 and 4, and citation to a recent study.

claim: The responses to a mixture of banana odor and sucrose were stronger than those to component stimuli in taste sensilla.
source: We found that the responses to a mixture were stronger than those to component stimuli (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by tip recording data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Responses to banana odor and sucrose recorded in the same sensillum were positively correlated.
source: While the strength of responses varied across sensilla, responses to banana odor and sucrose recorded in the same sensillum were positively correlated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: GRNs function as an odor-taste multisensory integrator.
source: These results suggest that GRNs function as an odor-taste multisensory integrator.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The addition of banana odor increased PER to sucrose, especially at low concentrations.
source: Although banana odor could not evoke PER on its own at this concentration (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), we found that the addition of banana odor increased PER to sucrose, especially at low concentrations where sucrose alone can only induce unreliable PER (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The enhancement of PER by banana odor was observed even after removing the olfactory organs.
source: Importantly, this enhancement was observed even after removing the olfactory organs (Figure 6B), indicating that the superadditive integration takes place in GRNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There is a clear division of labor between olfactory and gustatory organs in sensing stimuli with distinct physical properties in terrestrial animals.
source: In terrestrial animals, it has been considered that there is a clear division of labor between the two types of chemosensory organs in sensing stimuli with distinct physical properties; the olfactory and gustatory organs sense volatile and non-volatile chemicals, respectively.

claim: Odorants and tastants are defined by the identity of cognate organs.
source: Therefore, although odorants and tastants are defined by the identity of cognate organs, they are used interchangeably with volatile and non-volatile chemicals.
evidence: This is a statement about conventional terminology in the field.

claim: Volatile chemicals are within the molecular receptive range of GRNs.
source: However, we found using calcium imaging and electrophysiological recording that GRNs directly detect odorants, and this drives a classical taste-induced feeding behavior, PER, as well as increased food consumption. A previous study has also hinted that odors alone evoke PER (Oh et al., 2021). Thus, volatile chemicals are within the molecular receptive range of GRNs and should also be regarded as tastants based on the conventional definition.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and citation to a previous study.

claim: Volatile chemicals should be regarded as tastants based on the conventional definition.

claim: GRNs are engaged in non-contact chemo-sensing.
source: Critically, this indicates that GRNs are engaged in non-contact chemo-sensing as well, a behavioral strategy distinct from contact-based chemo-sensing.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the finding that GRNs respond to volatile odors.

claim: A previous study applying base recording reported that I-type sensilla do not respond to odorant molecules dissolved in solution.
source: A study applying base recording, an electrophysiological technique to record from individual taste sensilla, had reported that I-type sensilla do not respond to odorant molecules dissolved in solution (Hiroi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A recent study found that S-, I-, and L-type sensilla respond to a variety of odors applied as vapor.
source: However, a recent study using the same method found that S-, I-, and L-type sensilla respond to a variety of odors applied as vapor (Dweck and Carlson, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: GRNs respond to odors applied in both dissolved and vapor forms.
source: Here, we found that GRNs respond to odors applied in both ways in agreement with Dweck and Carlson, 2023.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings and comparison with a recent study.

claim: The physiological condition of sensilla may be one of the factors underlying the discrepancy between studies.
source: Although the reason behind the discrepancy is not entirely clear, one possibility is the difference between the preparation used in different studies; whereas Hiroi et al. used a severed head preparation, as well as Dweck and Carlson used immobilized, intact flies. Because we noticed in preliminary experiments that stimulus-evoked GRN spikes become weaker over time in a hea- only preparation where hemolymph circulation is lost, the physiological condition of sensilla may be one of the factors underlying the discrepancy.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations from preliminary experiments.

claim: A difference in genotype or genetic background may underlie the discrepancy between studies.
source: Another possibility is a difference in genotype or genetic background. We found that the strength of odor-evoked PER is different between genetic backgrounds with w1118 exhibiting weaker PER than Dickinson wild-type (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), implying that odor responses of GRNs vary across genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This is speculation based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Odor responses of GRNs vary across genetic backgrounds.
source: We found that the strength of odor-evoked PER is different between genetic backgrounds with w1118 exhibiting weaker PER than Dickinson wild-type (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), implying that odor responses of GRNs vary across genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Odor tuning of sugar-sensing GRNs was different between this study and Dweck and Carlson, 2023.
source: Furthermore, odor tuning of sugar-sensing GRNs was different between our study and Dweck and Carlson, 2023, which used different genetic lines.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's findings and a recent publication.

source: Although we have observed odor-evoked PER in Drosophila simulans as well, further study is required to examine the generality as well as the variability of GRN odor responses across genotypes and species.

source: Furthermore, we found that OBPs enriched in the labella modulate odor-evoked PER, suggesting that OBPs in this taste organ not only link tastants with gustatory receptors (Jeong et al., 2013; Swarup et al., 2014), but also mediate detection of odors.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the RNAi knockdown experiments and citations to previous literature.

claim: PER was evoked by all the tested odors albeit to different extents.
source: PER was evoked by all the tested odors albeit to different extents, and this likely reflects the broad odor tuning of Gr5a GRNs that drive PER (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The broad odor tuning of Gr5a GRNs likely reflects why PER is evoked by all tested odors.

claim: During foraging in the air, olfactory receptor neurons locate a potential food source together with other sensory systems.
source: A likely benefit can be discussed by considering foraging behavior under natural settings. During foraging in the air, olfactory receptor neurons that are more sensitive to odors locate a potential food source together with other sensory systems.
evidence: This is speculation about the ecological significance of the findings.

source: Given that the olfactory system most likely has already guided the animal to palatable food, keeping the GRNs broadly tuned to odors is an efficient mechanism to enhance PER.
evidence: This is speculation about the adaptive significance of the findings.

source: Once PER brings the labella into contact with the food, GRNs act as a multisensory integrator to make a decision on food intake (Figure 6).

source: Enhancing PER to aversive odors might also be adaptive, as animals often need to carry out the final check by tasting a trace amount of potentially dangerous substances to confirm that those should not be consumed.
evidence: This is speculation about the adaptive significance of the findings.
